title: The Strong Tower and the Power of the Tongue
summary: The chapter begins with the person who cuts himself off from others and the fool who only wants to air his opinions. It sets the name of the LORD, a strong tower for the righteous, beside the rich man's imagined fortress, and gathers sayings on hasty answers, lawsuits, gifts, offended brothers, and a wife as a good gift. At its center is the claim that life and death are in the power of the tongue, and it closes with the friend who sticks closer than a brother.
story: The collection continues to probe the social life of the wise person. Chapter 17 dealt with conflict; chapter 18 deals with the ways people protect themselves and the places they run for safety. Some retreat into isolation (verse 1), some into their own opinions (verse 2), some into wealth (verse 11), some into the many companions who cannot really help (verse 24). Against all of these the chapter sets one true refuge, the name of the LORD (verse 10). Speech remains a thread, since words are how people wound, defend, and connect.
historical:
Several sayings reflect the workings of Israel's legal system. Disputes were heard in the gate before elders, with each party stating his case. Verse 17 describes what every judge learned: the first speaker always sounds convincing until the other side cross-examines him. The law's insistence on hearing witnesses and investigating thoroughly (Deuteronomy 19:18) rests on the same insight. Verse 13 warns against answering before hearing the matter, a failing in judges and in ordinary conversation alike. Verse 18 mentions casting the lot to settle quarrels between strong opponents, an impartial method when the evidence could not decide (compare 16:33).

The picture of the strong tower in verse 10 would have been familiar from Israelite towns. Walls were reinforced with towers, and some cities had a fortified tower inside the walls as a last refuge. When Abimelech attacked the town of Thebez, its people fled into a strong tower in the city and shut themselves in (Judges 9:51).
cultural:
Verse 16 speaks of a gift that opens doors and brings a man before the great. In the ancient Near East, approaching a king or official usually required a gift. Jacob sent gifts ahead to Esau (Genesis 32:13-21) and later to the ruler of Egypt (Genesis 43:11), and the queen of Sheba brought gifts to Solomon (1 Kings 10:10). Such gifts were expected courtesy, distinct from bribes that perverted a judgment, though the line between them could blur.

Verse 8 compares gossip to choice morsels swallowed into the inmost being. The image is of delicacies eaten eagerly and digested deep inside, which is exactly how rumors are received and retained. The saying appears again, word for word, in 26:22. Verse 19's offended brother, harder to win than a fortified city, reflects the closeness and the fragility of family ties in a society where brothers often shared land and inheritance, and where a quarrel between them could last for generations, as the stories of Jacob and Esau, and of Joseph and his brothers, show.
literary: The chapter contains several deliberate pairings. Verses 10 and 11 set the name of the LORD as a strong tower beside the rich man's wealth as his fortified city, and the second saying adds the barbed phrase in his imagination: one refuge is real and the other only feels real. Verse 11 reuses the first line of 10:15, and verse 12 ends with the same line as 15:33. Verses 20 and 21 both use the image of eating the fruit of one's mouth, joining speech to its consequences. The chapter is framed by two sayings about companionship, the isolating man at the start and the man of many companions at the end. Verse 24 is difficult in Hebrew: the first line may mean that a man of many companions comes to ruin, or that some companions are only for company, and translations differ, but the second line's friend who sticks closer than a brother is clear.

outline.t: Deep words, partial judges, and the fool's mouth
The strong tower and the imagined wall
Hearing first, the broken spirit, and the other side of the case
Lots, offended brothers, and the power of the tongue
A wife, the poor man's plea, and a faithful friend

doctrines.note: The righteous run to the name of the LORD and are safe (verse 10). Faith in Proverbs is not abstract belief but a place a person runs in danger, and the chapter sets it against trust in wealth, which is safe only in the imagination (verse 11).

The human spirit can endure sickness, but a broken spirit is almost unbearable (verse 14). The chapter recognizes that people are more than bodies and that the inner life can be wounded in ways that outward strength cannot heal.
Wisdom listens before it answers (verse 13), seeks knowledge (verse 15), and hears both sides (verse 17). The fool, by contrast, delights only in airing his own opinions (verse 2).

words.note: Migdal, tower. The word names watchtowers in vineyards, defensive towers in city walls, and fortified strongholds. Verse 10 makes the LORD's name a tower of strength, a place of refuge the righteous can run into. The image is defensive and concrete: safety within walls when the enemy is at the gate.

Shem, name. In Hebrew thought a name is more than a label; it stands for the person's character, reputation, and presence. God's name is how he makes himself known and available to his people (Exodus 3:13-15; 34:5-7). To run to his name is to run to God himself as he has revealed himself.

Ohev, friend, literally one who loves. Verse 24 contrasts companions (re'im) with the ohev who sticks closer than a brother. The verb behind stays closer, dabaq, to cling, is the one used in Genesis 2:24 of a man holding fast to his wife and in Ruth 1:14 of Ruth clinging to Naomi. True friendship is a matter of loyal love.

Ruach, spirit. The word can mean wind, breath, or spirit, and in the Old Testament it often names the inner vitality of a person. Verse 14 contrasts a spirit that sustains a sick body with a crushed spirit that no one can bear, a striking recognition of the weight of inner despair.

christ: Verse 10's strong tower is picked up in the Psalms, where the LORD is a refuge and a strong tower against the enemy (Psalm 61:3), and the New Testament gives the name of the LORD a new focus. Peter and Paul both quote Joel's promise that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved and apply it to calling on Jesus (Acts 2:21; Romans 10:13). Peter told the council that there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). The friend who sticks closer than a brother (verse 24) has long been read by Christians as a picture of Christ's loyalty. That is a devotional application, not the verse's original meaning, but it fits the Jesus who promised to be with his disciples always (Matthew 28:20). Verse 21's claim that life and death are in the power of the tongue finds an echo in James's warning about the small member that sets a forest ablaze (James 3:5-6).

hard.q: Verse 22 says he who finds a wife finds a good thing. What about those who are single, or whose marriages are unhappy?
hard.a:
The saying celebrates marriage as a gift from God and a sign of his favor, echoing Genesis 2:18, where it is not good for the man to be alone. But like other proverbs it describes a general truth, not a universal rule. Proverbs itself is honest that marriage can be miserable: it warns about the quarrelsome wife (19:13; 21:9, 19; 25:24) and praises a prudent wife as a gift precisely because not every wife is one (19:14). Read as a promise that every marriage will be good, the verse is false; read as praise for a good marriage as one of God's great gifts, it is true.

The verse also does not say that being unmarried is a lesser state. Jesus himself was unmarried, and Paul, also unmarried, commended singleness as a calling that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:7-8, 32-35). Christians have long held both marriage and singleness to be honorable callings. The verse invites gratitude from those who have found a good spouse; it passes no verdict on those who have not.

questions: Verse 10 says the name of the LORD is a strong tower. Where do you tend to run first when you feel threatened?
Verse 13 says answering before hearing is folly and disgrace. What would it look like to listen fully before responding in your next disagreement?
Verse 21 says life and death are in the power of the tongue. Whose words have given you life, and whose words have wounded you most deeply?
